qs.q: Which genetic mutation accounts for the majority of cases of Adult Polycystic Kidney Disease (APKD)?
qs.e: Mutations in the PKD1 gene account for 85% of APKD cases, while PKD2 accounts for about 15%. The disease is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, not recessive or X-linked.

qs.q: What is the inheritance pattern of adult polycystic kidney disease (APKD)?
qs.e: APKD is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with mutations in PKD1 or PKD2. It does not follow an autosomal recessive or X-linked pattern.

qs.q: Which gene mutation accounts for approximately 85% of cases of adult polycystic kidney disease?
qs.e: Mutations in the PKD1 gene account for 85% of APKD cases, while PKD2 accounts for about 15%. PKHD1 is typically associated with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease.

qs.q: Besides the kidneys, which organ frequently develops cysts in approximately 30% of patients with adult polycystic kidney disease?
qs.e: About 30% of patients with APKD also have hepatic cysts, though liver function is usually normal. Cysts in the spleen or thyroid are not the primary extra-renal manifestation highlighted here.

qs.q: What serious intracranial vascular complication is associated with adult polycystic kidney disease?
o: Arteriovenous malformations producing focal seizure activity
Cavernous sinus thrombosis with associated cranial nerve palsy
Berry aneurysms that may cause subarachnoid hemorrhage
Subdural hematoma resulting from minor head trauma
qs.e: Patients with APKD can develop familial berry aneurysms which may lead to subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Arteriovenous malformations are not the classic genetic vascular lesion associated with this condition.

qs.q: Which therapeutic agent can be used to slow cyst formation in some patients with adult polycystic kidney disease?
o: Furosemide, a loop diuretic for volume control
Desmopressin, a synthetic antidiuretic hormone analogue
qs.e: The vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist, tolvaptan, can slow cyst formation in some patients with APKD. Furosemide is a loop diuretic used for volume management rather than altering cyst progression.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Polycystic Kidney Disease (PKD) is a genetic disorder causing multiple renal cysts that enlarge and impair kidney function. It presents with hypertension, hematuria, and progressive renal failure, often requiring lifelong monitoring.

sections.p: PKD is characterized by numerous fluid‑filled cysts arising from renal tubules, leading to enlarged kidneys. Diagnosis relies on imaging criteria and family history, with genetic testing when available.
b: Ultrasound criteria: ≥2 cysts in each kidney for age >30 (ADPKD)
MRI/CT can detect smaller cysts and assess total kidney volume
Genetic testing confirms PKD1/PKD2 mutations

t.b: Positive: multiple bilateral cysts meeting age‑specific thresholds; Negative: insufficient cysts, consider other cystic disease

sections.p: Severity is staged by total kidney volume (TKV) and eGFR, guiding prognosis and timing of interventions.
b: eGFR >60 mL/min/1.73 m²: stage 1–2; 30‑59: stage 3; <30: stage 4‑5

sections.p: PKD is primarily genetic, but secondary cystic disease can mimic it, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Autosomal dominant PKD (PKD1 ~ 85%, PKD2 ~ 15%)
Autosomal recessive PKD (PKHD1) – presents in infancy
Obstructive uropathy, reflux nephropathy, HIV‑associated nephropathy, schistosomiasis‑related cysts

t.b: Positive: multiple affected relatives across generations; Negative: consider secondary causes

sections.p: Patients often develop hypertension early, flank pain, hematuria, and progressive loss of renal function; extrarenal manifestations are common.
b: Hypertension before age 30 in ADPKD
Gross hematuria from cyst rupture
Progressive eGFR decline
Berry aneurysms, hepatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse

t.b: Systolic > 140 mmHg suggests early renal involvement; treat to <130/80

sections.p: Imaging, labs, and screening for extrarenal disease guide management.
b: Renal ultrasound or MRI for cyst burden
Serum creatinine/eGFR for function
Urinalysis for hematuria/protein
Screen for intracranial aneurysm in high‑risk

t.b: eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m² indicates CKD stage 3+; if unavailable, use creatinine clearance

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent care.
b: Sudden severe flank pain → cyst hemorrhage or infection
Rapid rise in creatinine → acute kidney injury
Neurologic deficit → ruptured berry aneurysm

t.b: Fluid collection with rim enhancement suggests infection; hyperdense cyst indicates bleed

sections.p: Treat underlying hypertension, manage complications, and prepare for renal replacement when needed.
b: ACE inhibitors or ARBs for blood pressure and proteinuria
Tolvaptan (V2‑receptor antagonist) slows cyst growth in selected patients
Antibiotics for cyst infection; avoid nephrotoxic drugs
Renal transplantation is definitive therapy

t.b: Lowers intraglomerular pressure, slows CKD progression; preferred over beta‑blockers for renal protection

sections.p: Regular monitoring slows progression and detects complications early.
b: Blood pressure check every 3‑6 months
eGFR and urinalysis annually
MRI TKV every 1‑2 years in rapid progressors
Screen for intracranial aneurysm every 5 years if family history

sections.p: Other cystic kidney diseases can mimic PKD on imaging.
b: Multicystic dysplastic kidney (congenital, unilateral)
Acquired cystic kidney disease in dialysis
Medullary sponge kidney (benign, often asymptomatic)

t.b: Early infancy suggests ARPKD or dysplasia; adult onset favors ADPKD

sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring or alarming.
b: Normal ultrasound in early ADPKD (cysts may be too small)
eGFR can stay >60 mL/min despite large cyst burden

t.b: Re‑image; cysts may become detectable later

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe flank pain, fever, or chills (possible cyst infection or hemorrhage)
Rapid rise in serum creatinine or oliguria (acute kidney injury)
New severe headache, visual changes, or loss of consciousness (possible ruptured berry aneurysm)

faq.a: No cure exists; treatment slows progression and manages complications.
Yes, ADPKD follows an autosomal dominant pattern; ARPKD is autosomal recessive.
Berry aneurysms occur in up to 10% of ADPKD patients and can cause fatal subarachnoid hemorrhage.
